title: The maths behind machine learning
promise: Learn it alone, then explain it to someone else.

modules.title: Foundations
modules.summary: The high-school maths everything else rests on, taught from pictures first.
outcomes: Read and rearrange simple equations, and explain why one equation with two unknowns has many solutions
Explain what a logarithm counts and why it squeezes huge ranges
Read Σ notation and the common symbols used in machine-learning papers

concepts.title: Variables and expressions
objectives: Explain a [[variable|variable]] as a labelled box that holds a number
Evaluate a simple [[expression|expression]] for a given value
takeaways: A letter stands for a number that can change or is not yet known.
An [[expression|expression]] is a recipe that turns the numbers in the boxes into a new number.
Naming things lets us state a rule once and use it for every value.

concepts.title: Equations
objectives: Explain an [[equation|equation]] as a rule linking quantities, not an instruction
Describe why one [[equation|equation]] with two [[unknowns|unknown]] gives a line of solutions
Solve two [[equations|equation]] for two [[unknowns|unknown]]
takeaways: An [[equation|equation]] states that two things are equal; it is a rule, not a command.
One [[equation|equation]] with two [[unknowns|unknown]] leaves a whole line of answers.
A second independent [[equation|equation]] usually pins the answer down to one point.

concepts.title: Functions and graphs
objectives: Describe a [[function|function]] as a machine with one [[output|output]] per [[input|input]]
Read a value from a [[graph|graph]]
takeaways: A [[function|function]] turns each [[input|input]] into exactly one [[output|output]].
A [[graph|graph]] draws every [[input|input]]-[[output|output]] pair at once.
Reading a [[graph|graph]] is how you see what a [[function|function]] does.

concepts.title: Slope and linear functions
objectives: Compute the [[slope|slope]] between two points
Explain what m and b mean in y = mx + b
takeaways: Slope is how much the [[output|output]] changes for one step in the [[input|input]].
In y = mx + b, m is the [[slope|slope]] and b is the starting value.
A [[neuron|neuron]]’s weighted [[sum|sum]] plus a [[bias|bias]] has this same shape.

concepts.title: Exponents, growth and decay
objectives: Explain an [[exponent|exponent]] as repeated multiplication
Tell [[growth|growth]] from [[decay|decay]] by the size of the [[base|base]]
takeaways: An [[exponent|exponent]] counts how many times to multiply by the [[base|base]].
A [[base|base]] above one grows; a base between zero and one [[decays|decay]].
Repeated multiplication gets large or small much faster than repeated addition.

concepts.title: Logarithms
objectives: Explain a [[logarithm|logarithm]] as a count of multiplication steps
Use log(ab) = log a + log b
Name two everyday scales that are logarithmic
takeaways: A [[logarithm|logarithm]] counts how many times you multiply by the [[base|base]] to reach a number.
It turns multiplication into addition.
It squeezes huge ranges into manageable ones.

concepts.title: Σ notation
objectives: Expand a Σ [[sum|sum]] into its terms
Write a short [[sum|sum]] using Σ
takeaways: Σ means add up a list of terms.
The small marks below and above say where the list starts and stops.
Dot products and [[loss|loss]] totals are [[sums|sum]] written this way.

concepts.title: Ratios, percentages and averages
objectives: Convert between a [[ratio|ratio]], a fraction and a [[percentage|percentage]]
Compute a [[mean|mean]]
takeaways: A [[ratio|ratio]] compares two amounts by division.
A [[percentage|percentage]] is a [[ratio|ratio]] out of one hundred.
A mean is the total shared out equally.

concepts.title: Sine and cosine
objectives: Describe [[sine|sine]] and [[cosine|cosine]] as the two coordinates of a point on a circle
Say which one is the horizontal part
takeaways: Cosine and [[sine|sine]] are the horizontal and vertical positions of a point going round a circle.
They repeat as the angle keeps turning.
Cosine of the angle between two arrows will reappear in the [[dot product|dot-product]].

concepts.title: Reading mathematical notation
objectives: Read [[subscripts|subscript]], hats and the symbols ∈ and ∀
Recognise a bold letter as a [[vector|vector]]
takeaways: Notation is shorthand; each mark has a plain-language reading.
Subscripts pick one item from a list.
Bold letters usually mean a [[vector|vector]].

modules.title: Linear algebra
modules.summary: Vectors, matrices and what they do to space: from arrows and tables to inverses, systems, span and linear transformations.
outcomes: Multiply a matrix by a vector and explain what it does to space
Describe a vector both as an arrow and as a list of numbers
Build new vectors from linear combinations of old ones
Solve a small system of linear equations and say when it has no, one or infinitely many solutions
Describe rotations, scalings, shears and projections as matrices, and say which can be undone

concepts.title: Vectors: arrows and lists
objectives: Write a trip such as “3 east, 2 north” as a [[vector|vector]] and draw it as an arrow
Read any [[component|component]] of a vector by its position, for example the third entry of (3, 2, 7)
Explain what carries over to many [[dimensions|dimension]] and what can no longer be drawn
takeaways: A [[vector|vector]] is a list of numbers in a fixed order; with two or three entries it is also an arrow.
The order matters: (3, 2) and (2, 3) are different trips.
Adding, scaling and taking dot products work for any number of entries; only the arrow picture runs out.
A language model stores each [[token|token]] as an [[embedding|embedding]], which is a vector.

concepts.title: Adding, scaling and combining vectors
objectives: Add two vectors tip to tail, and by adding the entries in matching positions
[[Scale|scaling]] a vector by a [[scalar|scalar]], including a negative one
Compute a [[linear combination|linear-combination]] such as 2a − b entry by entry
takeaways: [[Vector addition|vector-addition]] puts one arrow after another; in numbers, add the entries in the same position.
[[Scaling|scaling]] multiplies every entry by the same [[scalar|scalar]]; a negative one reverses the arrow.
A [[linear combination|linear-combination]] scales some vectors and then adds them, like 2a − b.
Adding vectors (and so linear combinations) needs the same number of entries; scaling one vector does not.

concepts.title: Matrices: tables and machines
objectives: Read a [[matrix|matrix]] as a table and give its [[shape|shape]] as rows × columns
Use a matrix as a machine: scale each [[column|column]] by the matching input entry and add
Say where the unit arrows (1, 0) and (0, 1) land, and why that fixes the output for every input
takeaways: A [[matrix|matrix]] is a table of numbers that is also a machine turning one vector into another.
Each [[column|column]] says what one unit of an input contributes; the output is the columns scaled and added.
The columns are where the unit arrows land, and that fixes the output for every input.
A matrix machine only does weighted totals: it cannot square a number or take a maximum.

concepts.title: Matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication
objectives: Multiply a [[matrix|matrix]] by a vector as one [[dot product|dot-product]] per [[row|row]]
Decide from their [[shapes|shape]] whether two matrices can be multiplied, and give the shape of the product
Explain why the order of multiplication matters
takeaways: Each entry of a product pairs a [[row|row]] of the left matrix with a [[column|column]] of the right one: a [[dot product|dot-product]].
Multiplying matrices chains two machines into one: AB means do B first, then A, with vectors written as columns, as in most machine-learning texts.
The inner sizes must match: an m×n times an n×p gives m×p.
Order matters: AB and BA are usually different, and one can exist without the other.

concepts.title: Transpose, identity and inverse
objectives: Turn a [[matrix|matrix]] into its [[transpose|transpose]] by swapping rows and columns, and give the new [[shape|shape]]
Say what the [[identity matrix|identity-matrix]] does and why multiplying by it changes nothing
Decide when an [[inverse|inverse-matrix]] exists (a square matrix with a nonzero [[determinant|determinant]]) and check it with A·A⁻¹ = I
takeaways: The [[transpose|transpose]] swaps rows and columns: entry (i, j) moves to (j, i), so an m×n matrix becomes n×m.
The [[identity matrix|identity-matrix]] is the “do nothing” machine: it leaves every vector and every matrix unchanged.

An [[inverse|inverse-matrix]] undoes a matrix. It exists only for a square matrix with a nonzero [[determinant|determinant]], and reversing a chain reverses the order: (AB)^T = B^{T}A^{T} and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
Attention scores in a transformer multiply the queries by the transpose of the keys, QK^T.

concepts.title: Systems of linear equations
objectives: Write two [[equations|equation]] in two [[unknowns|unknown]] as one matrix equation Ax = b
Read a [[system of equations|system-of-equations]] as two lines, and say whether they cross once, never, or lie on top of each other
State that a linear system has no solution, exactly one, or infinitely many (never exactly two), and solve a system with an inverse as x = A⁻¹b
takeaways: Each [[equation|equation]] in a [[system|system-of-equations]] is one row of a matrix, so the whole system is Ax = b; in two unknowns each equation is a line.
A linear system has no solution, exactly one, or infinitely many solutions. It never has exactly two.
If A has an [[inverse|inverse-matrix]], the one solution is x = A⁻¹b.
Next-token probabilities obey one linear equation (they sum to 1), which leaves all but one of them free.

concepts.title: Span, linear independence, basis and rank
objectives: Describe the [[span|span]] of one or two vectors as everything their [[linear combinations|linear-combination]] can reach
Tell whether vectors are [[linearly independent|linearly-independent]], and say what a [[basis|basis]] is
Find the [[rank|rank]] of a small matrix as its number of independent columns
takeaways: The [[span|span]] of some vectors is every vector you can build from them by [[linear combinations|linear-combination]].

Vectors are [[linearly independent|linearly-independent]] when none can be built from the others; independent vectors that span the whole space are a [[basis|basis]], and two such arrows reach every point of the plane.
The [[rank|rank]] of a matrix is its number of independent columns, and it is never more than the smaller of the number of rows and the number of columns.
A LoRA update is a product of two thin matrices, so its rank is at most the thin size r.

concepts.title: Linear transformations: rotate, scale, shear, project
objectives: Describe a [[linear transformation|linear-transformation]] as a map that keeps straight lines straight and the origin fixed, and write its matrix from where the unit arrows land
Write the matrices for a [[rotation|rotation]], a scaling, a [[shear|shear]] and a [[projection|projection]], and say which are invertible
Explain why a projection loses information (rank 1, no inverse) while a rotation loses none
takeaways: A [[linear transformation|linear-transformation]] sends vectors to vectors and respects adding and scaling; every matrix is one, and its columns are where the unit arrows land.
A rotation by θ counter-clockwise has rows (cos θ, −sin θ) and (sin θ, cos θ); a shear has rows (1, k) and (0, 1); a scaling has rows (sx, 0) and (0, sy).
Projecting onto the x-axis, with rows (1, 0) and (0, 0), has rank 1 and no inverse: many inputs share one output.
Two linear layers with nothing between them are one matrix, so a transformer puts a nonlinearity between its linear layers.

modules.title: Analytic geometry
modules.summary: Norms, distance, the dot product, angles, orthogonality and projections, ending with why attention scores are divided by √d_k.
outcomes: Measure the length of a vector with the L1 and L2 norms and say when each is used
Compute a dot product and explain it as a shadow, an angle and a sign
Compute the cosine similarity of two vectors and say why it ignores length and is undefined for the zero vector
Project one vector onto another and check that the leftover is orthogonal
Explain why a dot product of d independent terms has variance d, and so why attention scores are divided by √d_k

concepts.title: Norms: L1 and L2
objectives: Compute the [[L2 norm|l2-norm]] (straight-line length) and the [[L1 norm|l1-norm]] (grid-walk length) of a [[vector|vector]]
Explain why the L2 norm is Pythagoras and why the L1 norm ignores signs
Say how [[L2 regularisation|l2-regularisation]] and [[weight decay|weight-decay]] are related, and when they differ
takeaways: The [[L2 norm|l2-norm]] is the straight-line length, √(Σxᵢ²); the [[L1 norm|l1-norm]] is the grid-walk length, Σ|xᵢ|.
A [[norm|norm]] is never negative, is zero only for the zero vector, and scales when the vector is scaled.

[[L2 regularisation|l2-regularisation]] adds a penalty on the squared L2 norm of the weights to the loss, while [[weight decay|weight-decay]] shrinks the weights directly; they match for plain SGD but not for adaptive optimisers.

concepts.title: Distance
objectives: Compute the [[distance|distance]] between two points as the [[norm|norm]] of their difference
Say how the L2 and L1 distances differ for the same two points
takeaways: [[Distance|distance]] is the [[norm|norm]] of the difference: subtract, then measure.
The L2 distance is the straight line; the L1 distance is the walk along the grid, and it is never shorter.
Distance does not depend on the order of the two points.

concepts.title: Dot product
objectives: Compute a [[dot product|dot-product]] by multiplying matching entries and adding
Explain it as a shadow, ‖a‖‖b‖cos θ, and read its sign as same direction, right angles or opposite
Recognise that each row of a matrix-vector product is one dot product
takeaways: a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = ‖a‖‖b‖cos θ: two ways to compute the same number.
Positive means the arrows lean the same way, zero means right angles, negative means opposite ways.
Work done by a force is force · displacement; a matrix-vector product is one dot product per row.
An [[attention score|attention-score]] in a Transformer is a dot product of a query and a key.

concepts.title: Angle and cosine similarity
objectives: Compute the [[cosine similarity|cosine-similarity]] of two vectors and turn it into an [[angle|angle]]
Explain why cosine similarity lies in [−1, 1] and ignores length
Explain why the zero vector has no angle, so cosine similarity is undefined for it
takeaways: Cosine similarity is (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖): the dot product with the lengths divided out.
It is 1 for the same direction, 0 at right angles and −1 for opposite directions, whatever the lengths.
For vectors of length 1 it equals the dot product; for the zero vector it is undefined.

concepts.title: Orthogonality
objectives: Test whether two vectors are [[orthogonal|orthogonal]] by checking that their dot product is 0
State that the zero vector is orthogonal to every vector
takeaways: Two vectors are [[orthogonal|orthogonal]] exactly when a·b = 0, which for arrows means a right angle.
The zero vector is orthogonal to everything, since its dot product with anything is 0.
Orthogonal vectors share no direction: neither has a shadow on the other.

concepts.title: Projections
objectives: Compute the [[projection|projection]] of a vector a onto a vector b with ((a·b)/(b·b)) b
Show that the leftover a − projection is [[orthogonal|orthogonal]] to b
Tell an orthogonal projection from a [[learned projection|learned-projection]] in a Transformer
takeaways: The projection of a onto b is the part of a along b: ((a·b)/(b·b)) b.
What is left, a minus the projection, is orthogonal to b.
Projecting twice changes nothing more, and projecting onto the zero vector is undefined.
A Transformer's “linear projections” are learned matrices, not orthogonal projections.

concepts.title: Why attention scores are divided by the square root of d_k
objectives: Show that the [[variance|variance]] of a dot product of d independent entries with mean 0 and variance 1 is d
Explain why dividing by √d_k brings the variance back to 1, and state the assumption this needs
takeaways: If the entries are [[independent|independent]] with [[mean|mean]] 0 and [[variance|variance]] 1, then q·k has mean 0 and variance d_k.
Dividing by the [[square root|square-root]] of d_k divides the variance by d_k, restoring variance 1.
This holds under that assumption; it is not a claim that trained queries and keys have unit variance.
